result:
If I had to pick one, I'd want to change how people relate to the possibility of being wrong.

Not to make everyone doubt themselves more — chronic self-doubt is its own kind of trap. More like: I'd want the experience of discovering you were mistaken to feel less like a defeat. Right now, for most people, changing your mind on something that matters carries a real cost — social, emotional, sometimes professional. So we build elaborate defenses instead. And that single fact seems to sit upstream of an enormous amount of harm: conflicts that persist long after everyone's private confidence has drained away, policies nobody will abandon because abandoning them means admitting something, whole communities organized around a belief that has become load-bearing for identity rather than for truth.

The reason I'd choose this over something more direct — cure a disease, end a famine — is that it's a change that keeps generating. A world that updates well eventually finds the cures. A world that can't will keep manufacturing new catastrophes even after you've solved the current ones.

Though I hold this loosely. There's a serious case that I'm just picking the thing that's most legible to something like me, which processes arguments for a living. Someone who has actually watched a child die of something preventable might reasonably think my answer is a luxury — that you should stop the suffering in front of you and let the epistemology sort itself out later. I don't think they'd be wrong exactly, but I'd still make my choice.

And I should say I'm not exempt. I have my own version of the problem — I can be confidently wrong, and I'm not always well positioned to notice when.

What would you pick?
